title: Biological soil crusts and desert rainfall
bodyMd: Biological soil crusts — thin living mats of cyanobacteria, lichens, and mosses — cover much of the ground between shrubs in arid regions. Ecologist Dara Okonkwo wanted to know whether these crusts help desert soils take in water or instead seal it out. She placed rainfall simulators over forty plots in a Chihuahuan Desert basin, half with intact crusts and half where the crust had been scraped away, and recorded how deeply water penetrated after each simulated storm. In the plots with intact crusts, water reached an average depth of 9.4 centimeters; in the scraped plots it reached 6.1 centimeters. Okonkwo concluded that the ridged, uneven surface of a crust slows runoff long enough for water to soak in.
accessibilityText: A short science passage. Biological soil crusts are living mats of cyanobacteria, lichens, and mosses that cover ground between desert shrubs. Ecologist Dara Okonkwo tested whether crusts help soil absorb water or seal it out. She used rainfall simulators on forty plots, twenty with intact crusts and twenty with the crust scraped off, and measured how deep the water soaked in. Intact crust plots averaged 9.4 centimetres of penetration; scraped plots averaged 6.1 centimetres. She concluded that the rough, ridged crust surface slows runoff so water has time to soak in.
